name: Château Frontenac
label: Château Frontenac
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terrasse Dufferin' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Terrasse Dufferin' (relation/9923629): middle (428 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/32580: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fairmont Le Château Frontenac' (197 m across).
notes: The famous hotel dominating the Quebec skyline.

text.description: The Château Frontenac is the big copper-roofed hotel that dominates the Old Quebec skyline, and it has a fair claim to being the most photographed hotel in the world. It was designed by the New York architect Bruce Price for the Canadian Pacific Railway and opened in 1893. It has 18 floors and stands about 80 metres tall. It also sits on a high promontory above the St. Lawrence River, so it looks even taller than it is. The style is called Châteauesque. The steep roofs, round towers, turrets, dormers and tall chimneys were inspired by medieval châteaux in France's Loire Valley, and the building's outline is deliberately uneven. That makes it very easy to photograph. The hotel was named a National Historic Site of Canada in 1981, and an earlier building, the Château Haldimand, stood on the site until it was demolished in 1892. The classic view is from Terrasse Dufferin, the boardwalk in front of the hotel. From there you see the full façade and the copper roof rising above the boards, with the river at your back. The boardwalk runs along the cliff edge, so you can try several framings. If you want a second angle, Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons looks down on the hotel and terrace with the skyline around them. Rue Dalhousie shows the hotel towering over older stone buildings on a cobbled street. The terrace gets very crowded in summer and during cruise season, so go early if you want a clear shot.
text.geographic_location: In the Upper Town of Old Quebec, on the southern side of Place d'Armes, right on the edge of the cliff above the Lower Town and the St. Lawrence River. Terrasse Dufferin wraps around its eastern side.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops listed for this spot, so head on foot for Old Quebec's Upper Town and Place d'Armes. From the hotel, walk to Terrasse Dufferin on its eastern side and look for the Dufferin kiosk on the boardwalk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole façade and the roof in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers, turrets and copper roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terrasse Dufferin (boardwalk directly in front of the hotel, near the Dufferin kiosk). The Château Frontenac's full façade and copper roof rising above the boardwalk, with the St. Lawrence River behind you as you face the hotel. Face north-west towards the hotel, with the St.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it upwards, or the sides will converge. Use the boardwalk rail or boards as a foreground line. Winter toboggan runs on the terrace can end up in the frame, so check the edges before you shoot. For a different view, try Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons from above, which involves stairs or a walk up from the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the roof to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the copper roof isn't washed out. In crowds, take a few shots in a row and keep the one with the fewest people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour buses arrive. One local guide gives about 6:30 AM in summer and 8:30 AM in winter. The terrace is very crowded in summer and during cruise season.

text.access_note: Terrasse Dufferin is a free, open public boardwalk; check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside the hotel.
claims_not_in_sources: Early-morning sun would be behind you and falling on the façade when you face north-west from the stand-here point.
Tilting a phone upwards makes vertical lines appear to converge, and gridlines help keep them straight.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky colour and avoid washing out a bright roof.

name: Montmorency Falls
label: Montmorency Falls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'La Baronne' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Belvédère de la Baronne' (node/10984461552): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1946396: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfall higher than Niagara, just east of the city.

text.description: Montmorency Falls drops 83 m into the St Lawrence River, which is about 30 m higher than Niagara Falls. That height is what makes it so photogenic. A tall white ribbon of water falls against a dark cliff, with the river and the western end of Île d'Orléans beyond. The falls sit at the mouth of the Montmorency River, about 12 km from the heart of old Quebec City, inside a protected park. In summer the water can take on a yellowish tint from the iron in the riverbed, which gives the scene a warmer colour. For a closer, quieter angle, head to La Baronne, a clifftop observation deck beside the falls. From the deck the cascade looks tight and close, and you can also take in the gorge and the view across toward Île d'Orléans. Guides call it quieter than the bridge. If you have time, two other spots in the park give different views. The suspension bridge over the top of the falls looks down on the drop with the river and the Quebec City skyline behind. The Escalier Panoramique gives an upward view through the spray. Take a few frames from each and compare. The park has staircases, a suspension bridge and a funitel, so allow time to walk between viewpoints. Early morning is the calmest time to photograph.
text.geographic_location: Montmorency Falls lies on the boundary between the Beauport borough of Quebec City and Boischatel, where the Montmorency River meets the St Lawrence. It is about 12 km from the heart of old Quebec City, and the viewing area is inside Montmorency Falls Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check local travel options before you go. The falls are about 12 km from the heart of old Quebec City. Once inside the park, La Baronne is reached on foot from the Manoir area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cascade, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the gorge and the view across toward Île d'Orléans.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on La Baronne (clifftop observation deck beside the falls). A tighter, closer angle on the cascade from the clifftop, with the gorge and the view across toward Île d'Orléans.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the cascade on one of the vertical lines, with the cliff edge along a lower line so the drop looks tall. Use telephoto for a close crop of the water. Use the ultra-wide when you want the gorge and the distant island in the same frame. For a different view, the suspension bridge looks down the drop toward the river and the skyline, and the Escalier Panoramique looks up through the spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the foam keeps its detail instead of turning plain white. A Live Photo can capture the movement of the water. Wipe the lens often if there is spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive, according to one photo guide.

text.access_note: The falls are inside Montmorency Falls Park, which charges admission, and the staircase can be closed in winter or for repairs, so check the official site before you go.

name: Plains of Abraham
label: Plains of Abraham
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pierre-Dugua-De Mons Terrace' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Pierre Dugua de Mons' (pois).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Large historic park above the river.

text.description:
The Plains of Abraham is the large, open stretch of parkland that runs west from the Citadelle and the old city walls, on a plateau above the St. Lawrence River. It is best known as the place where British and French forces fought on 13 September 1759, a battle that was over in about half an hour and left Quebec City in British hands. The park was created on 17 March 1908 and became the first National Historic Site in Canada. Today it covers about 98 hectares, roughly 2.4 km long, and around four million people visit each year for walks, sport and concerts.

On a phone, the Plains photograph best as a wide view rather than a single landmark. The place to shoot from here is Pierre-Dugua-De Mons Terrace, which looks across the green space and the river towards the Château Frontenac and the old city skyline. That gives you open lawn and trees in the foreground, the water in the middle and the rooftops beyond. If you have time, two other overlooks nearby offer different postcard views: Parc du Bastion-de-la-Reine looks over the river and the rooftops, though the Plains only partly appear, and Jardin Jeanne-d'Arc adds flower beds in front of the river view. Wear comfortable shoes, as the park is big and the walking paths are long.
text.geographic_location: The Plains of Abraham lie inside the Battlefields Park in Quebec City, stretching west from the Citadelle and the old city walls along the plateau above the St. Lawrence River.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Citadelle and the old city walls and head west onto the Plains. The Plains of Abraham Museum, at 835 Wilfrid-Laurier Avenue, is the park's reception centre and a handy starting point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the lawns, the river and the skyline in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Château Frontenac and the old city rooftops in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pierre-Dugua-De Mons Terrace. A wide view across the Plains of Abraham and the St. Lawrence River toward the Château Frontenac and the old city skyline. From the terrace the view takes in the park, the St.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether the sky or the river matters more. Use the grass or a path edge in the foreground to add depth. For a wider sweep, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily. If you have time, Parc du Bastion-de-la-Reine and Jardin Jeanne-d'Arc offer different postcard views of the river and rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the skyline to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky looking washed out. If a bright sky makes the foreground too dark, lower the exposure slightly and check the result before moving on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Check the weather first, because a clear day shows the river and the distant skyline best.

text.access_note: The Plains of Abraham is a public park used by visitors all year, but the museum, tours and events may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Place Royale
label: Place Royale
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Royale' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Royale' (way/27073360): middle (56 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q844351: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic square in Lower Town with Notre-Dame-des-Victoires.

text.description: Place Royale is a small cobbled square in the Lower Town (Basse-Ville) of Quebec City, and it is where Samuel de Champlain founded the settlement in 1608. That is why it is often called the cradle of French civilization in America. The stone houses around it went up after a fire in 1682 destroyed the earlier wooden buildings. A bust of Louis XIV, a replica of the 1686 original, gives the square its name. The church front of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires closes one side. It photographs well because the church, the cobbles and the steep-roofed stone houses all fit in one frame, and the buildings have been restored to their French colonial look. From there the church front sits across the cobbles with the bust and the surrounding houses beside it. Go early if you can: the square is at its most atmospheric and least crowded before about 9 AM. Late afternoon can bring warmer light onto the facades. If the square is busy, rue Dalhousie may offer a quieter, closer-in angle on the same buildings; check it on the map first. Businesses or events may occupy parts of the square and block part of the view.
text.geographic_location: Place Royale is in the Lower Town (Basse-Ville) in the centre of Quebec City. The church of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires stands on the square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so it is best reached on foot in the Lower Town (Basse-Ville). From there, the middle of the square lies to the south, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the church, the cobbles and the houses together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the church front. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the church door, the bust or the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Royale (eastern end of the square, facing the church). Wide view of the Notre-Dame-des-Victoires church front across the cobbled square, with the Louis XIV bust and the surrounding stone houses in frame. The middle of the square lies to the south of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the church front centred, with the cobbles filling the lower part of the picture. Include the bust and a few house fronts at the sides to show the size of the square. Keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean. If businesses, events or people block the view, rue Dalhousie may offer a quieter, closer-in angle; check it on the map first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church front to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few shots in a row, as people often walk through the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9 AM, when the square is quietest. Late afternoon can give warm light on the facades.

text.access_note: Place Royale is a public outdoor square, but businesses and events can occupy parts of it, so check for events beforehand if you need a clear view.

name: Notre-Dame de Québec Basilica-Cathedral
label: Notre-Dame Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Parc de l'Hôtel-de-Ville' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/103862161: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Quebec City' (103 m across).
notes: Oldest parish church in North America north of Mexico.

text.description: Notre-Dame de Québec is the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Quebec, and it sits right in the heart of Old Québec. Its calm, pale stone façade is neoclassical and looks very tidy in a phone photo. The tower and the symmetry give you clear lines to work with. The history is also unusually deep for North America. A chapel built by Samuel de Champlain stood on this spot in 1633, and the church is often described as the oldest in Canada. It was made a minor basilica in 1874 and is now a National Historic Site of Canada. The building has been rebuilt after fires, including one in 1759 and another in 1922. The present façade dates from a reconstruction proposed in 1843. The best outdoor view is from Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville, the square in front of the cathedral. From there the church is framed by the open space, with the Seminary of Quebec partly visible behind it on the left and older buildings around the edges. That gives you a photo with a sense of place, not just a close-up of a wall. A second option is Rue de Buade, which runs beside the church. From there you can take angled shots of the stone façade. Keep your phone level and upright so the walls do not lean inwards, and take a few frames at different distances.
text.geographic_location: In Old Québec, at 16 rue de Buade. The square in front of it, Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville, is the main outdoor setting for the cathedral.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so make your way to Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville in Old Québec by whatever route suits you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole façade along with the square and the buildings around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the church. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the tower and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville. The cathedral framed by the square, with the Seminary of Quebec partly visible behind the church to the left and other older buildings around the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the church up with the vertical lines so it looks straight. Keep a little of the square and the surrounding buildings in the frame to show the setting. For a different angle, walk to Rue de Buade, beside the church, and take angled shots of the stone façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright so the façade keeps its detail. Try panorama only if people are not walking through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day for the quietest square. In the evening there can be live music and street performers, which adds atmosphere but also people in your photos.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or photography rules inside.

name: Dufferin Terrace
label: Dufferin Terrace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De Mons' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Terrasse Dufferin'.
notes: Boardwalk with views over the St. Lawrence River.

text.description: Dufferin Terrace is a long boardwalk that runs along the cliff edge beside the Château Frontenac, with the St. Lawrence River open below. It photographs well because it gives you a strong leading line, the boardwalk, with the grand hotel on one side and the wide river on the other. This is on Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace, an elevated lookout above the boardwalk. From there you see the length of Dufferin Terrace below, with the Château Frontenac and the river beyond. The terrace was built under the Marquess of Dufferin, then Governor General of Canada, and opened on 28 June 1879. Parks Canada looks after it. Along the boardwalk are six named gazebos, which make pleasing repeating shapes in a wide shot. At the southern end is a 150-metre ramp that becomes a toboggan run during the Quebec Winter Carnival. Cruise season and summer street performers can make the boardwalk busy, so expect people in your frame. If you want a close view of the boardwalk running toward the hotel, the Monument Samuel-de-Champlain makes a good second spot. Plateforme du Roi is another, for open river views along the terrace edge. Take your time and let people walk out of the frame before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Dufferin Terrace is in the historic heart of Quebec City, wrapped around the Château Frontenac on the cliff edge above the St. Lawrence River. It runs from the hotel towards the Citadelle.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops for this spot, so head for the Château Frontenac. Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace is reached by a path or stairs from near the hotel. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the boardwalk, the hotel and the river together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the terrace is busy or you want the whole length of the boardwalk and the hotel in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gazebos and the hotel towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace (elevated lookout above the boardwalk, reached by a path or stairs from near the Château Frontenac). The length of Dufferin Terrace below, with the Château Frontenac and the St. Lawrence River beyond. It is the classic higher-angle view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the boardwalk up with a grid line so it leads the eye towards the hotel. Keep the river as a calm band along one edge. For a different view, Plateforme du Roi gives open river views framed by the boardwalk. The Monument Samuel-de-Champlain gives a close view with the statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hotel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode only if you can hold the phone steady, and wait for passers-by to clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer and kinder to the light than midday. Cruise season and summer street performers can make it crowded.

text.access_note: The lookout and the boardwalk are open public spaces, but parts of the terrace can be steep, cobbled or gravelly, and the walkway under the terrace is not always open, so check the official site before you go.

name: Petit Champlain
label: Quartier Petit Champla
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Escalier Casse-Cou' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Escalier Casse-cou' (way/27073398): middle (37 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W27369585 (Rue du Petit-Champlain): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Picturesque shopping street at the foot of the cliff.

text.description: Petit Champlain is the little cobbled lane at the foot of the cliff in Quebec City, lined with shopfronts and historic buildings. It photographs well because the street is narrow and gently receding, so shop signs, strung lights and old facades all lead the eye in one direction. The classic postcard angle is from the Escalier Casse-Cou (the Breakneck Stairs), looking down toward the street. The stairs have several landings, so you can step aside and take your time without blocking anyone. For a different view, walk down to Rue du Petit-Champlain itself, where the lane looks lovely with few people in front of the lens if you arrive early. Nearby, a large painted mural shows scenes from the neighbourhood's history and daily life. It works as a backdrop for a close shot of the lane, but there may be barriers and fencing there during restoration work, so it may be partly blocked. The stairs and the street get very busy from mid-morning, so an early start makes the biggest difference. Keep your phone's gridlines on to hold the vertical lines of the buildings straight as the street falls away below you.
text.geographic_location: Petit Champlain is in Quebec City, at the foot of the cliff. The Escalier Casse-Cou is the staircase that runs down toward it.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the receding street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the buildings and lights in the frame. The narrow lane suits it well.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Escalier Casse-Cou (middle and landings of the stairs, looking down toward the street). The receding line of Rue du Petit-Champlain below, with its shopfronts, strung lights and cobbles, framed by the historic buildings at the foot of the cliff.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the street in the centre or on one third. Keep the building edges vertical so they don't lean. Use a landing to stand clear of other people, and keep the steps' handrail or edge in the foreground if you want depth. For a second angle, go down to Rue du Petit-Champlain and shoot along the lane while it is still quiet.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit shopfronts to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the strung lights stay bright and the facades keep their colour. Hold the phone steady against the handrail or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 7 to 8 am, when the steps are nearly empty. Early evening gives better light if you don't mind people in the frame.

text.access_note: The stairs and the street are public places that need no ticket, but check the official site before you go for any closures or building works.

name: Gare du Palais
label: Gare du Palais
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Jean-Pelletier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Jean-Pelletier' (way/291177803): middle (230 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1789873399: the OpenStreetMap point 'Québec'.

text.description:
Gare du Palais is Quebec City's railway and coach station, and it looks more like a small fairytale château than a transport hub. It was built in 1915 by the Canadian Pacific Railway and designed in the château style of the Loire, with steep copper roofs, turrets and an ornamental clock high on the roof. It has a similar look to the Château Frontenac hotel. The station closed to passengers in 1976 and reopened in 1985 after a major renovation. It was later given Heritage Railway Station status, in 1992.

From there you see the whole façade across open grass, with the Éclatement II fountain by Daudelin as a sculptural foreground. The pointed roofs and turrets make a strong outline, so the shot works even on a plain day.

Keep the whole building in the frame and use the fountain to add depth. If you want detail, move closer to the arcaded ground floor, or zoom in on the turrets and dormers. A quieter, greener view of the station and the neighbouring former post office block is also possible from the same square. The fountain is not always running, and the station has had renovation work, so what you see may differ a little from older pictures.
text.geographic_location: Gare du Palais stands in downtown Quebec City, on rue de la Gare-du-Palais. Place Jean-Pelletier is the public lawn in front of it.
text.directions_text: Start from downtown Quebec City and head for rue de la Gare-du-Palais. Check the map to be sure you have the right place. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole façade and the fountain together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close to the fountain and want it large in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the turrets, dormers and roof clock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Jean-Pelletier (grassy area facing the train station). The chateau-style station façade with the Éclatement II fountain in the foreground. From here the château-style façade fills the background and the Éclatement II fountain sits in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the fountain on the lower third, with the turrets and steep roofs above. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the turrets stay straight. For a quieter, greener view, include the lawn and the neighbouring former post office block at the side of the frame. For a close-up, move towards the arcaded ground floor and zoom in on the roofs and dormers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the roofs stay detailed. Check whether the fountain is running before you plan a shot around it. If it is, a Live Photo can catch the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: There is no single best time. Daylight, when the stone and copper roofs are clearly visible, gives the clearest view of the façade.

text.access_note: The lawn in front of the station is an open public square with no charge, but check the official site before you go in case renovation work affects views of the façade.

name: Citadelle of Quebec
label: La Citadelle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De Mons' (way/392156895): middle (104 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5877711: large area 'The Citadel of Quebec' (641 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Citadelle is a star-shaped stone fortress on top of Cap Diamant, the rocky headland over the St. Lawrence River, right beside the Plains of Abraham. It is still an active military base, home to the Royal 22e Régiment since 1920. The present fortress was built between 1820 and 1850 and sits inside Old Quebec, which became a World Heritage Site in 1985. That mix of heavy stone walls, a clifftop setting and the river below is what makes it work on a phone screen.

The best frame is not from inside the fortress. Château Frontenac, the Dufferin boardwalk and the river are all nearby and can be seen from the terrace. The fortress itself lies about 293 m to the south-west of this point.

Keep the walls in the lower part of the picture and let the sky fill the top. If you want a second angle, the Promenade des Gouverneurs has the walls on one side and the river on the other, and Terrasse Dufferin gives a view back along the clifftop. Because the Citadelle is a working military site, the grounds are visited on guided tours, and photography is restricted in some areas.
text.geographic_location: The Citadelle stands on Cap Diamant in the Old Quebec Historic District, on the edge of the Plains of Abraham and above the St. Lawrence River. The terrace for the photo sits beside its outer walls, not far from Château Frontenac and the Dufferin boardwalk.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot. The terrace is in Old Quebec, near Château Frontenac, and can be reached on foot. Follow the walls rather than cutting across the grounds, which are reached on guided tours. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the walls sit comfortably in the frame with some sky above. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the wall in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull a stretch of wall out of the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons (on the elevated terrace beside the Citadelle's outer walls). The Citadelle's stone walls in the foreground, with Château Frontenac, the Dufferin boardwalk and the St. Lawrence River beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the wall along the lower third, with the sky above it. Keep the horizon level, as the walls will exaggerate any tilt. If you have time, try the Promenade des Gouverneurs or Terrasse Dufferin as another angle on the same fortress.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Live Photos can catch people walking along the wall for a bit of life in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone.

text.access_note: The Citadelle is an active military site, so its grounds and buildings are visited on guided tours and photography is restricted in some areas; check the official site before you go, including for the Changing of the Guard dates.

name: Observatoire de la Capitale
label: Observatoire Capitale

text.description:
The Observatoire de la Capitale is a viewing spot in Quebec City. Places like this can photograph well because a high vantage point lets you capture a wide scene and then pick out details with the zoom. That gives your phone more to work with than a street-level view usually does.

The phone icon on the map is at the observatory itself, so you take your photos from the spot, not from somewhere nearby. Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of a single landmark. Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant details.

If you shoot through glass, hold the phone flat against the surface and keep your hand or a dark jacket around the lens to cut reflections. Check the official site for current access details.
text.geographic_location: The Observatoire de la Capitale is in Quebec City.
text.directions_text: Use the map to navigate to the observatory. Once you are there, you are at the phone icon on the map, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole view, then use the default lens (1x) for a natural-looking shot. Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a spot with a clear view and no people in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon on a gridline so the scene does not look tilted. Include a foreground element to give depth. For a sweeping scene, try panorama and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: If you shoot through glass, press the phone flat to it to cut reflections. Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset usually gives softer light and warmer colours. Night mode can work after dark if you hold the phone steady against a surface.

text.access_note: Check the official site for current access details.

name: Parliament Building
label: Parliament Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale' (node/4988781279): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/196002: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hôtel du Parlement' (185 m across).
notes: Seat of the National Assembly of Quebec.

text.description:
The Parliament Building is the home of Quebec's National Assembly. It is an eight-floor Second Empire building, designed by Eugène-Étienne Taché and built between 1877 and 1886. The Assembly first met here in March 1884, two years before the work was fully finished. The façade is tall, formal and decorated, and it sits just outside the walls of Old Quebec. It is very easy to frame on a phone.

The best-known picture is taken from Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale, the square in front. The Tourny Fountain fills the foreground and the Parliament's façade rises behind it. That gives you a layered photo, with water and sculpture at the front and the grand building behind. The city's heritage commission describes the square as an ideal place to see both the Parliament and the western ramparts. Reviewers say the fountain looks good from across the boulevard and that it is lit at night.

The fountain stands on a roundabout, so take care crossing the road to find your angle. The square is also used for events. In winter the Carnaval's Ice Palace is built there, and it can block the view, so be ready to move along the pavement. If you want a second picture, walk up to the grounds in front of the building. There the façade is framed by lawns, gardens and bronze statues. Keep the shots simple: one wide scene, then one closer shot of the fountain or a statue.
text.geographic_location: On Parliament Hill (the Colline Parlementaire district), just outside the walls of Old Quebec, in the La Cité-Limoilou borough. The building faces Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale.
text.directions_text: Head for Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale, just outside the walls of Old Quebec. Cross Boulevard Honoré-Mercier with care, as the fountain sits on a roundabout. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the façade behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole front in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale (across Boulevard Honoré-Mercier from the fountain). The Tourny Fountain in the foreground with the Parliament's Second Empire façade rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on the lower third, with the building filling the upper two thirds. Keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone level. For an alternative, walk to the grounds in front of the building and frame the façade between the lawns, gardens and bronze statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit fountain and the sky do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, because the fountain lighting is bright against the dark sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or after dark, when the fountain is lit. Daytime also works, but check whether event stands or the winter Ice Palace are in the square.

text.access_note: The square in front is an open public space. Check the official site for current access to the grounds and the building.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep a tall, formal façade straight in a phone photo.
Night mode benefits from a steady hand or resting the phone on something solid.

name: Musée de la civilisation
label: Musée de la civilisati
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2546008681: the OpenStreetMap point 'Musée de la Civilisation de Québec'.
notes: Museum of history and society in the Old Port.

text.description:
The Musée de la civilisation sits in the historic Old Quebec area, close to the Saint Lawrence River. It was designed by the architect Moshe Safdie and opened to the public on 19 October 1988. The older Banque de Paris and Maison Estèbe buildings on Saint-Pierre street were worked into the museum's structure. That mix of old and new is what makes the building interesting to photograph: you can show a modern design and a historic streetscape in the same frame.

The museum holds more than 225,000 objects covering art, society and ethnography, and it has permanent and temporary exhibitions, so there is plenty to see if you go inside. For photographs, though, the outside is the main draw. Look for the lines of the walls, the contrast between stonework and newer surfaces, and the way the building meets the street.

The phone icon on the map coincides with the museum's mapped position, so you are photographing the building from very close. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens to fit more of the façade in, and keep your phone level so the vertical lines do not lean. Step back along the pavement and switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. The 2x zoom is handy for picking out details such as windows, stone textures or the join between old and new parts.

If you want pictures inside, rules on photography can vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Quebec area of Quebec City, near the Saint Lawrence River, in a museum that incorporates older buildings that stood on Saint-Pierre street.
text.directions_text: The spot data lists no nearby Underground, tram or station stops, so plan your approach to the Old Quebec area near the Saint Lawrence River using a map app on your phone and look for the Musée de la civilisation. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map coincides with the museum's mapped position, so there is no extra walk to the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole façade from close range, then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use 2x or more for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Because you are so close, step back to the far side of the pavement if you can, to fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls stay straight. Include a little of the street to show how the modern museum sits among the older buildings. Then take a closer shot at 2x of a detail, such as a window or stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon daylight is usually kinder to stonework than harsh midday sun. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for current visitor information and any rules on photography inside the museum.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer and better for photographing stonework than midday sun.
Photography rules inside the museum may vary, particularly for temporary exhibitions.

name: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec
label: MNBAQ
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3616083: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musee national des beaux-arts du Quebec' (342 m across).
notes: Art museum on the Plains of Abraham.

text.description: The Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec is Quebec City's national art museum. It sits inside National Battlefields Park and is made up of several linked buildings rather than one block, which gives you plenty of different pictures. The oldest part is the Charles Baillairgé Pavilion, designed in 1867 as a prison and used for that purpose until 1970. It is now part of the museum. The Gérard-Morisset Pavilion, the first building made for the museum, is in Beaux-Arts style, with carved reliefs on its facade by Joseph-Émile Brunet. It opened to the public in June 1933. A recent addition, the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion, opened in 2016. It was designed by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture and is built largely of glass and steel, with a glass-enclosed entrance from Grande Allée. It stands next to Saint-Dominique Church, so old stone and modern glass appear together in one frame. The collection runs to over 40,000 works from the 16th century to today, mostly from Quebec or by Quebec artists. For photographs, look for contrasts: the formal stone facade against the park's greenery, the glass reflecting the sky, and the church beside the new building. Walk around a little before choosing your frame. The complex is large, and each pavilion looks quite different. Keep your phone level so the long straight edges of the glass and stone don't lean.
text.geographic_location: In National Battlefields Park, just off Grande Allée, in Quebec City. The Pierre Lassonde Pavilion is next to Saint-Dominique Church.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so start from Grande Allée, where the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion has its entrance, and head into the park to the museum complex. If you are coming from further away, ask for the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion entrance on Grande Allée. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the museum grounds. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main views of the pavilions. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the glass pavilion and long facades when you are close. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the carved reliefs, the church next door, or the contrast between old and new buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Use it as your starting point, then walk a short way out along the park paths and turn back so that a whole pavilion fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the glass and stone with them so the buildings stand straight. Include a strip of grass or trees in the foreground to give a sense of scale and show that the museum sits in a park. Try one frame that holds the glass building and Saint-Dominique Church together, then a closer one of the Beaux-Arts stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or glass is bright, so the facade doesn't wash out. Use the ultra-wide close to buildings, and check the edges of the picture for stretched lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as morning or a bright overcast day, helps keep reflections on the glass manageable. At dusk, try night mode while the buildings are lit.

text.access_note: The museum itself is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for gallery access and visiting arrangements; the surrounding grounds are in National Battlefields Park.
